explanation: In standard German main clauses, the conjugated verb ('lerne') must always occupy Position 2. You may start with 'Ich' or with 'Heute' as long as the verb stays in Position 2.
When an adverb of time ('Heute') takes Position 1, the subject ('wir') moves immediately behind the conjugated verb ('trinken') so the verb remains in Position 2.
The conjugated modal verb ('kann') occupies Position 2, while the main action verb ('sprechen') is sent to the end of the sentence in its infinitive form.

english: He gets up at seven o'clock.
germanTarget: Er steht um sieben Uhr auf.
acceptableOrders: Er steht um sieben Uhr auf.
Um sieben Uhr steht er auf.
explanation: With separable verbs like 'aufstehen', the conjugated base verb ('steht') stays in Position 2, while the prefix ('auf') is positioned at the very end of the clause.

english: Are you coming to class today?
explanation: In German Yes/No questions (Entscheidungsfragen), the conjugated verb ('Kommst') moves to Position 1, directly followed by the subject ('du').

english: She does not understand the sentence.
explanation: When negating the entire verbal action or a specific definite direct object ('den Satz'), 'nicht' is placed at the end of the main clause.
The subject noun phrase ('Mein Bruder') occupies Position 1, followed directly by the conjugated verb ('arbeitet') in Position 2.

english: We eat fresh bread every morning.
germanTarget: Wir essen jeden Morgen frisches Brot.
acceptableOrders: Wir essen jeden Morgen frisches Brot.
Jeden Morgen essen wir frisches Brot.
grammarRule: Time before Object in Standard Word Order
explanation: Adverbs of time ('jeden Morgen') generally precede the direct object ('frisches Brot') in natural German sentence rhythm.
